progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m6-b02: a mutagen raises the chance of DNA damage; damage becomes a mutation when it is copied before it is repaired; UV joins neighbouring bases (thymine dimer); chemicals in tobacco smoke can attach to bases. From bio-m6-b05: a mutation in a body cell is copied into its daughter cells and can contribute to cancer. From b06: environmental causes are acquired and come from outside the body. From Year 11 (Module 2 and 4 basics): alveoli and gas exchange need a large surface; arteries carry blood from the heart; red blood cells carry oxygen on haemoglobin. Not assumed: exposure (as a defined term), carcinogen, COPD, plaque, dose, pack-years, latency, mesothelioma, macrophage.
progression.startsWith: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003. Yet each year, hundreds of Australians are still diagnosed with mesothelioma, a cancer that asbestos can cause. So how can a harm show up decades after the exposure stopped? And why do some people who breathed the same dust never get sick? That's today's question: how does environmental exposure cause disease?
progression.stopsAfter: using the exposure, change, effect spine; defining exposure as real contact including amount and duration; explaining three different pathways from one exposure, tobacco smoke (carcinogens damage airway-cell DNA, and mutations in genes that control division can start a tumour; inflammation and white blood cell enzymes destroy alveolar walls, with mucus build-up, giving COPD; damaged artery lining, plaque, carbon monoxide on haemoglobin and nicotine raising heart rate increase heart attack and stroke risk); explaining dose and calculating pack-years; explaining latency, with asbestos fibres that persist, frustrate macrophages and release reactive chemicals for decades before mesothelioma; explaining why exposure raises probability rather than guaranteeing disease (repair, immune clearance, chance, other exposures, interacting exposures); explaining why population-wide exposure reduction lowers disease, with Australian smoking and SunSmart; applying this to a smoking and lung cancer graph (latency) and to a named UV case without claiming every exposure causes disease.
progression.nextLesson: another exposure everyone has every day, what we eat: how nutrition changes disease risk (bio-m8-b08). Cancer itself, cell-cycle control and spread: bio-m8-b09.

teaching.task: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003, yet hundreds of Australians are still diagnosed with mesothelioma each year. How can a harm appear decades after the exposure stopped, and why do some exposed people never get sick?
teaching.causalExplanation: Earlier, you sorted the causes of non-infectious disease, and environmental causes come from outside the body. Here's how they actually make people sick. Every case follows one spine. First, an exposure: real contact with a harmful agent, including how much and for how long. Next, a change in cells or tissue. Then, an effect on health. Let's run tobacco smoke through it, because one exposure can lead to three different diseases. Pathway one is lung cancer. Smoke carries carcinogens, chemicals that raise the risk of cancer. They reach the cells lining the airways and attach to their DNA. You've seen what happens next: if that damage is copied before it's repaired, it becomes a mutation. When mutations build up in genes that control cell division, a cell can start dividing when it shouldn't. That can be the start of a tumour. Pathway two doesn't need a mutation at all. Smoke irritates the airways, so they stay inflamed for years. White blood cells gather and release enzymes that digest the thin walls between the tiny air sacs. Many small sacs merge into fewer, bigger ones, so there's much less surface for gas exchange. Mucus builds up too, because the hair-like cilia that sweep it out are damaged. Together this is COPD, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and the lost walls don't grow back.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003. Earlier, you sorted the causes of non-infectious disease, and environmental causes come from outside the body. Pathway one is lung cancer. Pathway two doesn't need a mutation at all. Pathway three is in the blood vessels. So what decides how much risk? First, dose: how much of the agent gets in, over how long. Second, time. So why do many heavy smokers never get lung cancer, while some people who've never smoked do? Because exposure raises the probability, not the certainty. That's also why a risk isn't a verdict on one person. Two exam questions. Smoking fell steadily from 1945, but lung cancer kept rising until the early 1980s, then fell, decades behind. Second. UV is absorbed by DNA in skin cells and joins neighbouring bases, so the DNA kinks. So for any environmental disease question, name the exposure and its dose, describe the change in cells or tissue, link it to the effect, then explain why it's a risk, not a certainty.
teaching.openingDecision: Australia banned asbestos at the end of 2003. Yet each year, hundreds of Australians are still diagnosed with mesothelioma, a cancer that asbestos can cause. So how can a harm show up decades after the exposure stopped? And why do some people who breathed the same dust never get sick? That's today's question: how does environmental exposure cause disease?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. The graph shows illustrative trends for one population of men: the percentage who smoked, and the rate of new lung cancer cases, from 1945 to 2020. Describe how the timing of the two trends differs. Then explain the difference. Pause here to answer. Second. A gardener has worked outdoors in Queensland for thirty years without sun protection. Explain how this repeated UV exposure can increase the risk of melanoma. Then explain why a co-worker with similar exposure may never develop it. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ2-01 (p 57): "investigate the causes and effects of non-infectious diseases in humans, including but not limited to:" with the listed example "diseases caused by environmental exposure". Causes: scenes 2 to 7. Effects: scenes 3 to 5 and 7 (tumour, COPD, heart attack and stroke risk, mesothelioma). Inquiry question: "Do non-infectious diseases cause more deaths than infectious diseases?" (not answered here; g01 and b10 use death data).

design.visualSystem: One pathway strip owns the bottom fifth of the frame from scene 2 to scene 9: three coded boxes "exposure → change in cells or tissue → effect", each filling with a small thumbnail and two to four words for the current case, so the spine is always visible. Above it, one painted plate or matched pair at a time with callouts. Tobacco smoke's three pathways (scenes 3 to 5) branch from one "tobacco smoke" exposure box into three change boxes, the earlier two dimming. A coded risk dial (a semicircle gauge marked "low" to "high", with no numbers) sits at the upper right from scene 6 to scene 8 and moves on dose, latency and the modifying factors. No people, hands or faces: smoke is coded grey wisps; the asbestos worker is a fibre-cement sheet plate; the gardener in attempt 2 exists only in the card's words. Coded elements are limited to the strip, the dial, the dose bars, the lottery tickets, the attempt graph, wisps, dots, arrows, chips and tags. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.

scenes.visualReference: the card stays. On "Smoking fell steadily from 1945" the grey line brightens and "the percentage who smoked" underlines; on "kept rising until the early 1980s" the amber line to its 1982 peak brightens and "rate of new lung cancer cases" underlines; a coded bracket spans 1945 to 1982, label "about 35 years". Answer (a) writes: "Smoking fell from 1945; lung cancer rose until about 1982, then fell. The cancer trend lags by decades." On "latency" answer (b) builds on the cues: "latency: mutations take decades to build up", "cancers from past smoking still appeared", "falls once fewer people had smoked for long". On "classic mistake" a chip "the peaks don't match, so smoking isn't the cause" writes and takes a scribble cross, small text "a lag is what latency predicts". Settle one second.
